question: What does the elimination period in disability insurance determine?
options: How long the insured must be disabled before benefits become payable
The maximum duration of benefits
The policy renewal date
The amount of the monthly benefit
explanation: The elimination period is the waiting period after disability begins before benefits become payable. A longer elimination period generally reduces premium but requires the client to fund a longer income gap.

question: A client has a 90-day elimination period and only two weeks of emergency savings. What is the main planning concern?
options: The client may lack cash to cover expenses before benefits start
Benefits will necessarily end after 90 days
The policy cannot cover sickness
The insurer will automatically shorten the waiting period
explanation: The client must be able to finance living expenses during the elimination period. The waiting period affects when benefits start, not how long they can continue.

question: Two otherwise similar disability policies have 30-day and 120-day elimination periods. Which will generally have the lower premium?
options: The 120-day policy
The 30-day policy
They must cost exactly the same
Premium is unrelated to the elimination period
explanation: A longer waiting period shifts more short-duration disability risk to the insured, so it generally lowers the premium, all else equal.

question: What does the benefit period specify in an individual disability policy?
options: The maximum period for which qualifying disability benefits can be paid
The time before underwriting begins
The period during which premiums are refunded
The number of days allowed to change beneficiaries
explanation: The benefit period is the maximum duration of benefits for a qualifying disability, subject to the contract, such as two years, five years or to a stated age.

question: A 35-year-old professional wants protection against a disability that could permanently end her career. Which feature is most important?
options: A long benefit period, potentially to a stated retirement age
The longest available elimination period regardless of savings
Accidental death coverage only
A dental reimbursement maximum
explanation: A long-term disability can last for decades. A longer benefit period protects against this severity risk, subject to affordability and policy terms.

question: Under a true own-occupation disability definition, what is the central question when assessing total disability?
options: Can the insured perform the substantial duties of the insured's own occupation as defined by the contract?
Can the insured perform any job at minimum wage?
Has the insured reached retirement age?
Has the insured exhausted all savings?
explanation: Own-occupation wording focuses on the insured's ability to perform the duties of the occupation specified by the contract. Exact wording varies, so the contract must be reviewed.

question: Why is an any-occupation disability definition generally more restrictive than an own-occupation definition?
options: Benefits may depend on inability to perform another occupation for which the insured is reasonably suited under the contract
It covers only accidental injuries
It always has a shorter elimination period
It pays only hospital expenses
explanation: Any-occupation wording broadens the work the insurer may consider when determining whether the insured remains disabled, making qualification more restrictive.

question: A surgeon loses fine motor control but can teach medicine. Why could an own-occupation definition be particularly valuable?
options: The surgeon may qualify based on inability to perform surgical duties even if able to work in another occupation, depending on the contract
It guarantees benefits for unemployment
It removes the elimination period
It guarantees all medical expenses
explanation: Highly specialized professionals may suffer a severe economic loss even while capable of other work. Own-occupation wording can address that risk, subject to the exact policy definition.

question: What is residual disability coverage designed to address?
options: A partial loss of income caused by reduced work capacity after sickness or injury
Only complete paralysis
Unemployment unrelated to health
Routine prescription expenses
explanation: Residual disability benefits can replace part of an income loss when the insured can still work but has reduced earnings because of disability.

question: Before disability, a client earned $10,000 per month. After returning part-time because of the disability, earnings are $6,000. What concept is most relevant to a residual benefit calculation?
options: The percentage loss of earned income
The client's mortgage balance only
The insured's life insurance death benefit
The number of dependants only
explanation: Residual benefits commonly relate the disability-caused income loss to pre-disability earnings, subject to the policy formula and thresholds.

question: What is the purpose of a recovery benefit in some disability contracts?
options: To continue limited benefits during economic recovery after medical recovery when the covered disability still causes an income loss
To pay a life insurance death benefit
To reimburse every medical expense
To eliminate underwriting
explanation: Some policies recognize that income may take time to recover even after the insured can resume full duties. Recovery benefits depend on the contract's conditions.

question: What is the purpose of a recurrent disability provision?
options: To specify when a later disability from the same or related cause is treated as a continuation rather than a new claim
To guarantee annual premium refunds
To convert disability insurance to life insurance
To exclude all recurring illnesses
explanation: A recurrent disability clause can prevent a new elimination period when a related disability returns within the contract's stated time, subject to its terms.

question: What does a waiver-of-premium provision generally do during a qualifying disability?
options: Waives required policy premiums after the contractual conditions are met
Increases the monthly benefit every month
Refunds all premiums paid since issue
Ends the policy
explanation: Waiver of premium helps keep coverage in force without required premium payments while the insured satisfies the policy's disability conditions.

question: What is the main purpose of a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) rider on disability benefits?
options: To help benefits keep pace with inflation during a long claim
To reduce the elimination period
To guarantee future insurability before disability
To reimburse medical deductibles
explanation: COLA provisions can increase benefits during a qualifying long-term disability according to the contract's inflation measure or formula.

question: A 28-year-old expects income to rise substantially over the next decade. Which disability feature can help preserve the ability to increase coverage later without new medical evidence?
options: Future increase or future insurability option
Recurrent disability provision
Waiver of premium
Accidental death rider
explanation: A future increase option can permit additional disability coverage at specified times if financial underwriting requirements are met, without fresh medical evidence, subject to the rider.

question: What is the key distinction between guaranteed renewable and non-cancellable disability coverage?
options: Guaranteed renewable coverage generally permits class-wide premium changes, while non-cancellable coverage generally locks contractual premiums and prevents unilateral cancellation while conditions are met
Guaranteed renewable policies can be cancelled solely because the insured files a claim
Non-cancellable policies have no exclusions
There is no meaningful distinction
explanation: Both forms strengthen renewability, but non-cancellable wording generally provides stronger premium guarantees. Exact rights depend on the contract.

question: Why does occupation matter in disability underwriting?
options: Different occupations have different disability incidence, duties and return-to-work risks
Occupation determines the beneficiary
Only office workers can buy disability insurance
Occupation determines life expectancy only
explanation: Insurers classify occupations because physical demands, hazards, stability and ability to return to work affect disability risk and available contract terms.

question: Why does an insurer usually limit an individual disability benefit to a percentage of earned income rather than insure 100% of income?
options: To reduce overinsurance and preserve an incentive to return to work
Because disability benefits can never exceed $1,000
Because all benefits are taxable
Because insurers ignore income during underwriting
explanation: Disability insurance is designed to replace part, not normally all, of earned income. Benefit limits help control moral hazard and coordinate with other coverage.

question: A self-employed applicant reports highly variable earnings. What information is especially important when determining an appropriate disability benefit?
options: Documented earned income over a representative period and existing disability coverage
The applicant's life insurance beneficiary
The market value of the applicant's home only
The applicant's credit-card limit
explanation: Financial underwriting verifies sustainable earned income and existing coverage so the proposed benefit is supportable and does not create overinsurance.

question: An applicant has a prior knee disorder. Which underwriting outcome could allow coverage to be issued while limiting that specific risk?
options: A policy exclusion relating to the knee
Automatic payment of a knee claim
Removal of all policy definitions
A guaranteed retirement pension
explanation: Depending on severity and underwriting rules, an insurer may issue coverage with an exclusion rather than decline the entire application.

question: Why should an advisor review an employer's group disability plan before recommending individual coverage?
options: Existing benefits affect the client's income-replacement gap, definitions, waiting periods and total available coverage
Group coverage guarantees the client needs no individual insurance
Individual insurers ignore group benefits
Group disability is always portable after employment ends
explanation: A proper needs analysis considers existing group LTD and STD benefits, their limits and definitions, and what happens if employment ends.

question: A client earns a high salary but the employer LTD plan has a monthly benefit maximum well below the plan's stated income percentage. What risk does this create?
options: The maximum may create a substantial income-replacement shortfall
The employer plan will automatically increase without limit
The client will receive 100% of salary
The maximum affects only life insurance
explanation: Group plans often combine a percentage formula with a dollar maximum. Higher-income employees can therefore have a larger uninsured gap.

question: Why is portability an important issue when comparing group and individual disability insurance?
options: Group coverage may end or change when employment ends, while personally owned coverage can generally continue subject to its terms
Individual coverage always ends when employment changes
Group coverage can never change
Portability affects only beneficiaries
explanation: Employment-linked benefits may be lost when the client changes jobs. Individual coverage can provide continuity independent of a particular employer.

question: An employee pays the full premium for an individual disability policy personally and receives benefits under that policy. What is the general Canadian tax treatment of qualifying benefits?
options: They are generally received tax-free
They are always taxed as salary
Only half is tax-free
They are treated as capital gains
explanation: Benefits from personally funded individual disability insurance are generally received tax-free. Tax treatment depends on who paid premiums and the arrangement, so plan details matter.

question: An employer pays all premiums for an employee wage-loss replacement plan and does not include those premiums in the employee's income. What is the general tax concern when benefits are paid?
options: Benefits are generally taxable to the employee under the applicable wage-loss replacement rules
Benefits are always tax-free
Benefits are capital gains
The employer receives the benefits
explanation: Employer-funded wage-loss replacement benefits are generally taxable to the employee, subject to the Income Tax Act and the structure of the plan.

question: Why must an advisor avoid saying simply that 'disability benefits are tax-free'?
options: Tax treatment depends on the policy or plan structure and who pays the premiums
All disability benefits are taxable
Tax treatment depends only on age
Tax treatment is chosen by the beneficiary
explanation: Individual personally paid coverage and employer-sponsored arrangements can produce different tax outcomes. The funding structure must be established before describing net benefits.

question: A client wants disability coverage equal to monthly living expenses. Which expenses should the advisor consider first?
options: Essential recurring costs such as housing, food, debt payments and family obligations, adjusted for available resources
Only entertainment spending
Only income tax
Only the life insurance premium
explanation: Disability needs analysis starts with the cash flow the client must maintain during a loss of earned income, then considers existing resources and benefits.

question: A client has six months of liquid emergency savings. How might that affect selection of an elimination period?
options: The client may be able to accept a longer elimination period to reduce premium, if appropriate
It requires the shortest elimination period
Savings determine the disability definition
Savings eliminate the need for long-term coverage
explanation: Strong liquid reserves can fund the initial waiting period, potentially allowing a longer elimination period. Long-term disability risk still remains.

question: A client has almost no emergency savings but can afford a higher premium. Which design change most directly reduces the period the client must self-fund after disability begins?
options: A shorter elimination period
A shorter benefit period
A stricter disability definition
A lower monthly benefit
explanation: A shorter elimination period begins benefits sooner, though it generally costs more.

question: A client can afford either a very short elimination period with a two-year benefit period or a 90-day elimination period with benefits to age 65. The client has adequate emergency savings and is most worried about catastrophic disability. Which design better targets that risk?
options: The longer benefit period with the 90-day elimination period
The two-year benefit period solely because benefits start sooner
Neither policy can cover catastrophic disability
Only accidental death insurance
explanation: When short-term expenses can be self-funded, prioritizing a long benefit period can better protect against the financially severe risk of prolonged disability.

question: What is presumptive disability coverage intended to do?
options: Treat certain severe specified losses as total disability under the policy without requiring the ordinary duties test
Pay for every minor injury
Replace the elimination period in every claim
Guarantee coverage for unemployment
explanation: Policies may deem specified catastrophic losses, such as certain losses of sight or limbs, to satisfy total disability provisions. Exact triggers vary by contract.

question: What does a rehabilitation benefit in a disability policy generally support?
options: Approved services or programs intended to help the insured return to productive work
A life insurance death claim
Home purchase costs
Retirement savings contributions regardless of disability
explanation: Rehabilitation provisions may fund or support approved retraining, therapy or return-to-work services when permitted by the contract.

question: Why might mental-health and substance-use wording require careful review when comparing disability policies?
options: Policies may differ in definitions, exclusions, limitations and benefit periods for particular conditions
Such conditions can never be covered
Every insurer must use identical wording
They affect only life insurance
explanation: Coverage for mental and nervous conditions or substance-related disabilities is contract-specific. Advisors should compare actual wording rather than assume uniform treatment.

question: A policy excludes disabilities arising from a named hazardous activity. What is the advisor's responsibility?
options: Explain the exclusion and its practical effect before the client relies on the policy
Tell the client exclusions are never enforced
Remove the exclusion without insurer approval
Ignore it if the premium is low
explanation: Material limitations must be explained so the client understands when benefits will and will not be payable.

question: A client changes from office administration to a much more hazardous occupation. Why should the policy terms be reviewed?
options: Occupation changes can affect risk and may interact with contractual occupation-change provisions
The beneficiary must automatically change
The elimination period always becomes zero
The policy automatically becomes life insurance
explanation: Some disability contracts contain provisions addressing occupational changes. The actual contract determines whether benefits or premiums can be affected.

question: What is the primary purpose of business overhead expense disability insurance?
options: To reimburse eligible business overhead expenses while an insured owner is disabled
To replace the owner's personal retirement income
To fund a death buy-sell agreement
To insure inventory against fire
explanation: Business overhead expense coverage helps keep a business operating by reimbursing covered fixed expenses during an owner's qualifying disability.

question: Which expense is more likely to fit the purpose of business overhead expense insurance?
options: Office rent
The disabled owner's personal groceries
A shareholder's vacation
The owner's life insurance death benefit
explanation: Business overhead coverage is designed for eligible business operating expenses such as rent and certain employee costs, not the owner's personal living expenses.

question: Two partners have agreed that if one becomes permanently disabled, the other will buy the disabled partner's interest. Which coverage is designed to fund that obligation?
options: Disability buy-sell insurance
Business overhead expense insurance
Individual dental insurance
Accidental death insurance
explanation: Disability buy-sell coverage provides funding for a business-interest purchase triggered by a qualifying disability under the agreement and policy.

question: Why should a disability buy-sell policy be coordinated with the shareholders' or partnership agreement?
options: The disability trigger, waiting period, valuation and funding structure should work together
The insurance policy automatically writes the legal agreement
The agreement determines medical underwriting
Coordination matters only after death
explanation: A mismatch between the legal agreement and insurance contract can create funding gaps or disputes. Definitions and timing should be aligned as closely as practical.

question: What is the purpose of key person disability insurance?
options: To protect a business against financial loss caused by the disability of an important employee or owner
To replace the key person's personal health plan
To insure the building
To pay a beneficiary at death
explanation: Key person disability insurance provides business liquidity when a crucial person's disability causes revenue loss or additional expenses.

question: A sole proprietor buys personal disability insurance and business overhead expense insurance. Why might both be needed?
options: One addresses personal income needs while the other addresses eligible business operating expenses
Both always pay exactly the same expenses
Business overhead coverage replaces personal income
Personal disability coverage reimburses only rent for the business
explanation: The coverages protect different cash flows: the owner's household income and the business's continuing overhead.

question: A claimant can work half-days and earns substantially less because of the covered disability. Which policy feature is most directly relevant?
options: Residual or partial disability benefit
Suicide exclusion
Life conversion privilege
Accidental death benefit
explanation: Residual or partial benefits are designed for disability-caused reductions in work capacity or income when the insured is not totally unable to work.

question: Why is proof of ongoing disability commonly required during a long claim?
options: Benefits remain conditional on satisfying the policy's disability definition and claim requirements
The insurer may change the beneficiary
The insured must reapply for the policy every month
Benefits become life insurance proceeds
explanation: Long-term benefits depend on continued eligibility. Policies therefore permit reasonable ongoing medical and financial evidence as specified by the contract.

question: A claimant's policy changes from an own-occupation definition for the first 24 months to an any-occupation definition afterward. What is the practical effect?
options: The claimant may face a stricter eligibility test after 24 months
Benefits automatically double after 24 months
The elimination period restarts every 24 months
The policy becomes non-cancellable
explanation: Some contracts change definitions after an initial period. A claimant who qualified initially may need to satisfy a broader any-occupation test later.

question: A client is covered by workers' compensation for workplace injuries. Why might individual disability insurance still be relevant?
options: Disability can arise from non-work illnesses or injuries, and public or workplace benefits may not fully replace income
Workers' compensation covers every illness and injury worldwide
Individual disability pays only workplace claims
The two products are identical
explanation: A comprehensive disability plan considers gaps in public and workplace programs, including non-occupational sickness and benefit limits.

question: Why should CPP disability benefits not be treated as a complete substitute for private disability insurance?
options: CPP disability has its own contribution and severe/prolonged disability eligibility rules and may provide less income than the client's need
CPP disability is available to every Canadian automatically
CPP disability replaces 100% of earnings
Private disability cannot coordinate with public benefits
explanation: CPP disability is an important public benefit but has statutory eligibility requirements and benefit levels that may leave a significant gap.

question: A client qualifies for several disability income sources. Why must the advisor review integration or offset provisions?
options: Some policies reduce benefits when specified other disability benefits are received
Every benefit always stacks without limit
Offsets apply only to life insurance
Offsets always increase the private benefit
explanation: Integration provisions can coordinate private benefits with specified public or group benefits to control total income replacement. The exact offsets are contractual.

question: What is the purpose of a coordination-of-benefits review when a client has both group and individual disability coverage?
options: To understand the total benefit available and identify any offsets, maximums or uninsured gaps
To choose a life insurance beneficiary
To eliminate all waiting periods
To make both policies identical
explanation: Multiple policies can interact through participation limits, offsets and financial underwriting. The advisor should assess the combined result rather than each policy in isolation.

question: A client receives a salary increase from $70,000 to $120,000 but never reviews disability coverage. What risk arises?
options: The existing monthly benefit may replace a much smaller percentage of current income
The policy automatically increases to 100% of income
The benefit period automatically extends
The elimination period disappears
explanation: Income growth can create an insurance gap. Regular reviews and future increase options can help keep coverage aligned with earnings.

question: A client is about to cancel an existing disability policy after applying for a new one. What is the prudent approach?
options: Keep existing coverage until the new policy is issued, accepted and its terms and exclusions have been reviewed
Cancel immediately to avoid overlapping premiums
Assume the new policy will be issued as applied for
Ignore new exclusions
explanation: Replacing disability insurance can expose the client to new underwriting, exclusions, definitions and contestability. Existing coverage should not be surrendered prematurely.

question: When comparing two disability policies, why is a lower premium not enough to establish suitability?
options: Definitions, exclusions, renewability, benefit period, riders and claim provisions can materially differ
All disability policies have identical wording
Premium is the only relevant factor
The insurer's logo determines coverage
explanation: Disability insurance is highly contract-specific. A cheaper policy can provide materially weaker protection, so features must be matched to client needs.

question: A client works in a specialized profession and says, 'I only care whether I can do my current job.' What should the advisor examine most closely?
options: The policy's exact total-disability occupation definition
The life insurance beneficiary clause
The dental deductible
The policy's accidental death amount
explanation: For a specialized professional, the occupation definition can determine whether benefits continue if the insured can work in another field.

question: A client has substantial investments but almost all are locked into long-term or illiquid assets. Why can disability insurance still be important?
options: A disability creates an ongoing cash-flow need, and selling illiquid assets may be costly or impractical
Net worth automatically replaces earned income
Disability insurance is only for clients with no assets
Illiquid assets guarantee monthly income
explanation: Needs analysis considers liquidity as well as net worth. Disability insurance can protect cash flow and reduce pressure to liquidate long-term assets at an unsuitable time.

question: A single client has no dependants but relies entirely on employment income to pay rent and debt. Does the client have a potential disability insurance need?
options: Yes, because disability threatens the client's own ability to meet ongoing expenses even without dependants
No, disability insurance is only for parents
No, only life insurance is relevant
Only if the client owns a business
explanation: Unlike life insurance, disability insurance primarily protects the insured's own income while alive. Dependants are not required for a meaningful need to exist.

question: A stay-at-home spouse performs childcare and household services but has no employment income. What is the key issue when considering disability coverage?
options: A disability could create replacement-service costs, but product eligibility and benefit design depend on insurer rules and insurable financial loss
No economic loss can ever occur
The spouse automatically qualifies for the same benefit as the working spouse
Only life insurance can address household-service costs
explanation: Unpaid household work has economic value, but disability products are often tied to earned income or specific homemaker provisions. Suitability requires checking available product rules.

question: A client asks whether disability insurance covers unemployment after a layoff. What is the best response?
options: Disability insurance generally requires a qualifying sickness or injury under the policy; ordinary unemployment is not a disability claim
Yes, every layoff is a disability
Only layoffs longer than 90 days qualify
Unemployment automatically triggers residual benefits
explanation: Disability income insurance protects against health-related inability or reduced ability to work, not ordinary job loss.

question: Why should the advisor distinguish sickness from injury provisions when reviewing a disability contract?
options: Waiting periods, exclusions or other terms can differ by cause under some contracts
Sickness is never covered
Injury is never covered
The distinction affects only the beneficiary
explanation: Coverage terms are contract-specific. Some products treat sickness and injury differently, so both causes should be reviewed against the client's needs.

question: A client says an illustration shows a future monthly disability benefit after exercising an increase option. What should the advisor clarify?
options: The client must satisfy the rider's contractual exercise conditions, including applicable financial requirements; an illustration is not itself a guarantee that every future increase will be available
Illustrations override the contract
No conditions ever apply to increase options
The future benefit is guaranteed regardless of income
explanation: Future increase riders preserve medical insurability only within their terms. Income and other financial requirements can still limit the amount available.

question: During a claim, a client asks the advisor to guarantee that the insurer will approve benefits. What should the advisor do?
options: Explain the claims process and help provide accurate documentation without promising an outcome the insurer must determine
Guarantee approval to reassure the client
Alter medical information to strengthen the claim
Tell the client not to disclose other benefits
explanation: The insurer adjudicates the claim under the contract. The advisor should assist accurately and professionally but must not misrepresent or guarantee the outcome.

question: A 42-year-old self-employed consultant earns $140,000, has three months of emergency savings, no group disability plan and depends on income for family expenses. What is the best first step?
options: Quantify the income-replacement need and cash reserves, then compare suitable benefit amounts, elimination periods, benefit periods and disability definitions
Recommend the cheapest policy immediately
Insure 100% of gross income without underwriting
Recommend accidental death coverage instead of disability insurance
explanation: A sound recommendation begins with needs analysis. The advisor should establish the financial gap and then match contract design, definitions and riders to the client's occupation, resources and budget.
